messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Emergency Contexts: Ambulances, Workplace: Workplace, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Threat: Night Vigilance: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
  Negative Appraisals: Identity Loss: I feel like I don't know myself anymore, Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

The first time an ambulance siren caught him mid-stroke, the brush skidded across the canvas and left a long, jagged scar of blue where a calm sky was meant to be. Kwame stared at the line for a long moment, his heart hammering against his ribs, and then he put the brush down and walked out of the garage he used as a studio. He did not pick the brush up again for three days. That was six months ago, and now he keeps the garage door closed even in summer, working in the stale heat because the street sounds are muffled in there. It does not help much. He still hears the sirens, and when he does, his body goes rigid, his shoulders drawing up toward his ears, his hands clenching into fists around whatever he is holding. He has come to believe that his body is waiting for something terrible to happen again, that it has learned a lesson his mind cannot unlearn.

The event itself was not a siren. It was a phone call. Kwame remembers the phone ringing at 2:47 in the afternoon, remembers the way the light fell across the kitchen table, remembers the exact weight of the receiver in his hand. His younger brother, Emmanuel, had collapsed at work. A blood clot. By the time Kwame reached the hospital, Emmanuel was gone. What haunts Kwame most is not the hospital room, which he barely remembers, but the moment of the phone call itself. He can see it in pictures: the yellow wall, the black cord of the phone, the dust motes floating in the sunbeam. But the feeling that comes with those images is not visual at all. Sometimes, without warning, the grief slams into him with the full force of that afternoon, even when he is looking at something completely unrelated—a grocery list, a paint chip, his wife’s face across the dinner table. There is no image attached to those moments, only the raw, suffocating weight of loss, as if his brother died five minutes ago.

At night, the vigilance is worse. Kwame has always been a sound sleeper, but now he lies awake listening to the house settle, his ears straining for something he cannot name. He knows it is irrational—his home is safe, his wife is beside him, the doors are locked—but he cannot convince his body. His muscles stay tight, his jaw clenched, his breathing shallow. He has started checking the locks twice before bed, then again at 2:00 AM when he wakes and cannot get back to sleep. What frightens him most is the feeling that he has become a stranger to himself. The man who used to laugh easily, who painted bold, bright canvases for local restaurants and private commissions, who looked forward to weekend barbecues with neighbors—that man feels like a photograph of someone else. Kwame does not know who he is anymore. He feels set apart, as though grief has placed him behind a sheet of glass where he can see other people living their normal lives but cannot reach them.

His work has suffered. He still takes commissions, but he paints mechanically now, without joy, and he has turned down three jobs that required him to work on site because the client’s office was near a hospital. He tells himself it is about traffic, about parking, but he knows the truth. The workplace itself has become a trigger. He paints alone in his garage, and even there, the word “loss” in a passing conversation on the radio can send him spiraling. A neighbor mentioned that her mother had passed away last spring, and Kwame had to excuse himself, his eyes burning, his throat tight with a grief that belonged to his own story but came roaring out at her kindness.

What finally brought him to seek help was his wife. She found him standing in the kitchen at 3:00 AM, staring at the phone. He did not remember walking there. She asked him what he was doing, and he could not answer. The next morning, she made an appointment for him. Kwame is not sure what he hopes for. He is afraid that talking about it will make the images sharper, the grief more frequent. But he is more afraid of spending the rest of his life feeling like a ghost in his own body, isolated and destroyed, waiting for a siren that has already come.
